title: Why Carboxylic Acids Are Acidic: Resonance and Substituents
subject: Chemistry
objective: Why vinegar fizzes with baking soda: the carboxylate ion shares its charge equally between two oxygens (resonance, arrow by arrow), which makes carboxylic acids stronger than phenols and alcohols; electron-withdrawing groups such as chlorine make them stronger still.

fill.q: Carboxylic acids liberate ____ gas from NaHCO₃.
The conjugate base of a carboxylic acid is the ____ ion.
A lower pKa means a ____ acid.
The effect by which Cl increases acidity is the ____ effect.

tf.explain: Phenol is too weak an acid.

tf.q: Both C–O bonds of the acetate ion have the same length.
Electron-donating groups increase the acidity of carboxylic acids.
tf.explain: They decrease it; electron-withdrawing groups increase it.

ar.a: Chloroacetic acid is stronger than acetic acid.
ar.r: Cl withdraws electrons (–I) and stabilises the carboxylate.

ar.a: Ethanol does not react with NaHCO₃.

num.q: How many equivalent resonance structures does the acetate ion have?

short.q: Explain with curved arrows why acetic acid is a stronger acid than ethanol.
short.solution: In acetate, an O⁻ lone pair forms C=O while the C=O π pair moves onto the other O: two equivalent structures share the charge. Ethoxide has no resonance: the charge stays on one O. The more stable anion makes acetic acid stronger.
